text.p: The Sydney 2000 Olympics will house all 15,300 athletes and officials in a high-tech "solar village", said the host Australian state government on Friday in unveiling the village design.
The A$470 million (US$371 million) village is in line with Sydney's commitment to a "green" Games, a cornerstone of its winning bid to secure the Summer Olympics.
"For the first time in modern Olympic history all of the athletes will be housed in one village," said New South Wales state premier Bob Carr.
Buildings would be designed to be energy efficient, water use would be minimised and solar cells would cut energy use by 60 percent compared with the average Australian home, Carr said.
Modern waste systems would also reduce energy use, while extensive landscaping with native plants would minimise the need for irrigation, he said.
Carr said the project would be designed, built and marketed by a consortium headed by local property developers Mirvac Ltd and Lend Lease Corp Ltd.
The Mirvac group defeated a tender from the rival Aurora Village consortium after the two were shortlisted in July.
The village will be built on 90 hectares (222 acres) of a larger site once used by the Royal Australian Navy, just one km (0.6 miles) from the Olympic stadium.
The site, containing a mix of temporary and permanent housing, would be sold off as a prestigious Sydney suburb at the end of the Olympic and Paralympic Games, Carr said.
The state government would contribute A$50 million to the project, but hoped to recoup A$17 million under a profit sharing agreement with the developers, he said.
About 2,200 jobs would be available during construction, with plans for 1,600 permanent jobs on a proposed industrial area at the north end of the village site.
Construction of the village will start mid-1997 and is the last major Olympic's infrastructure project to commence.
